name: URL Shortener
tagline: Grow a redirect service from one server to sharded storage and click analytics
summary: A URL shortener turns a long URL into a short code and redirects anyone who visits it. The problem looks trivial at 1,000 users and becomes a real distributed system at 10 million: reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude, every redirect is latency-sensitive, and short codes must be unique across many servers. Each step below keeps the previous design and adds only what the new scale demands.
requirements: Given a long URL, return a short unique code (about 7 characters).
Visiting the short URL redirects to the original with an HTTP 301/302 in well under 100 ms.
Codes must never collide, even when generated by many servers at once.
Links may expire after an optional TTL and can be deleted by their owner.
Click counts per link are available for analytics without slowing the redirect.
Abusive clients cannot exhaust the service by shortening or resolving in a loop.

steps.title: Single server
steps.problem: Nothing has broken yet — this is the starting point. The goal is the simplest system that meets the functional requirements: two endpoints and one table.
steps.why: One API process and one relational database are enough for a few thousand users and a handful of requests per second. PostgreSQL gives a unique constraint on the code column for free, so collisions are impossible by construction, and a single table (code, long_url, created_at, expires_at) is the entire data model. We deliberately avoid caches, queues and multiple servers until a measurement says we need them; every extra component is something to operate and debug.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Sends POST /shorten with a long URL and later GET /{code} to be redirected.

nodes.label: API Server
nodes.why: A single stateless process handles both endpoints; a 301/302 redirect is just an HTTP response with a Location header.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: One table keyed by code; a UNIQUE index guarantees no two links share a code.

steps.title: Many API servers behind a load balancer
steps.problem: A single API process is both the availability and throughput ceiling: one deploy or crash takes the whole service down, and CPU saturates during traffic spikes. Because the API is stateless, running several copies is the obvious fix — but now several servers generate codes at the same time.
steps.why: A load balancer spreads requests over N identical API servers, so a crash or rolling deploy no longer means downtime and throughput scales linearly until the database saturates. The subtle part is key generation. Two approaches work: (1) a counter — take the next value from a database sequence and encode it in base62 (0-9, a-z, A-Z), so 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes fit in 7 characters and collisions are impossible; (2) a hash — MD5/SHA of the long URL truncated to 7 base62 characters, which is stateless but can collide and must be checked (and re-salted) against the database. We choose the counter, handing each server a pre-allocated range of ids (e.g. 10,000 at a time) so servers do not contend on a single sequence. The cost is that counter-based codes are sequential and therefore guessable; if that matters, a random permutation or a hash is the alternative.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Unchanged — the client still sees one hostname.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Round-robins requests to healthy API servers and removes a failed one from rotation.

nodes.label: API Server 1
nodes.why: Owns a pre-allocated id range (e.g. 1–10,000) and encodes each id as base62, so no coordination is needed per request.

nodes.label: API Server N
nodes.why: Identical code, different id range; any number can be added behind the balancer.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Still a single instance; hands out id ranges with one atomic UPDATE and stores every link.

steps.title: Cache the redirect path
steps.problem: Adding API servers stopped helping: every redirect still does a SELECT, and with reads outnumbering writes 100:1 the single database is now the bottleneck. Popular links are looked up thousands of times a minute while the row never changes.
steps.why: The workload is read-heavy and links are effectively immutable, which is the ideal case for a cache-aside strategy: on GET /{code} the API checks Redis first, and only on a miss reads PostgreSQL and writes the result into Redis with a TTL. A small fraction of links receive most of the traffic, so a cache holding the hot set answers the large majority of redirects in sub-millisecond time and the database sees only misses and writes. The cost is a second stateful component and the classic invalidation question — here cheap, because a deleted or expired link is simply removed from Redis in the same request that updates the database. Memcached would serve equally well for pure key/value lookups; Redis is chosen because the next steps reuse it for rate-limit counters.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Unchanged.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Unchanged.

nodes.label: API Server 1
nodes.why: Implements cache-aside: GET code from Redis, fall back to the database on a miss, then populate the cache.

nodes.label: API Server N
nodes.why: Same logic; all servers share the one cache so a link warmed by one server is hot for all.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.why: Holds the most-visited links in memory with a TTL; absorbs the vast majority of redirect lookups.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Now sees only writes and cache misses, so one instance lasts much longer.

steps.title: Edge caching, rate limiting and read replicas
steps.problem: Three new failure modes appeared at once. Users far from the data centre see slow redirects because every request crosses the globe; a single abusive client can hammer POST /shorten or scrape codes and starve everyone else; and cache misses plus dashboard queries are again saturating the one database, now on read I/O rather than CPU.
steps.why: Each problem gets the smallest matching fix. A CDN in front of the load balancer caches redirect responses at the edge (a 301 for an immutable link is safely cacheable, a 302 with a short max-age when we want click counts), so most global users never reach our servers. A rate limiter at the entry point, backed by counters in the Redis we already run, caps requests per API key or IP and returns 429 instead of letting one client consume the fleet. Finally PostgreSQL streaming replication adds read replicas: writes still go to the primary, but cache-miss reads and analytics queries are routed to replicas. The costs are real: CDN caching means a deleted link may keep redirecting until the edge TTL expires, rate limiting adds a Redis round-trip to every request, and replicas are eventually consistent, so a link read immediately after creation may briefly 404 on a replica — we route reads for very fresh codes to the primary to hide that.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Now hits the nearest edge location instead of the origin.

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.why: Serves cached 301/302 responses close to the user; only misses travel to the origin.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Consults the rate limiter before forwarding so abusive traffic is dropped before it reaches an API server.

nodes.label: Rate Limiter
nodes.why: Sliding-window counters in Redis; returns 429 when a key or IP exceeds its budget.

nodes.label: API Server 1
nodes.why: Writes go to the primary; cache-miss reads go to a replica unless the code was created seconds ago.

nodes.label: API Server N
nodes.why: Same routing rules; the fleet is now sized for origin traffic only, which the CDN has shrunk.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.why: Reused for two jobs: the cache-aside store and the atomic INCR counters the rate limiter needs.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL Primary
nodes.why: Single writer keeps the unique-code guarantee simple; streams its WAL to replicas.

nodes.label: Read Replicas
nodes.why: Scale read I/O horizontally at the cost of replication lag measured in milliseconds to seconds.

steps.title: Shard by key and stream click analytics
steps.problem: Replicas scale reads but every write and the entire dataset still live on one primary; billions of links no longer fit its disk or its write throughput, and the id-range sequence on that single primary is a write hotspot. Meanwhile incrementing a click counter on every redirect has become a write per read, which defeats the whole caching layer.
steps.why: Two changes address the two problems. First, the links table is sharded horizontally: the shard is chosen by hashing the code (hash(code) mod N, or consistent hashing to make resharding cheaper), so a redirect knows exactly which shard to ask without a lookup. Code generation stays collision-free because each shard owns a disjoint id range whose base62 encoding never overlaps — the counter approach from step 2 now pays off, since a hash-based scheme would need a cross-shard uniqueness check. Second, redirects stop writing to the database at all: the API emits a click event to Kafka and returns immediately, and an analytics consumer aggregates events in batches into its own store. This keeps the redirect path at cache speed, lets analytics be rebuilt by replaying the log, and decouples reporting from serving. The costs are significant: cross-shard queries (all links for a user) require a secondary index or scatter-gather, resharding is an operational project, click counts are eventually consistent by seconds to minutes, and Kafka is a heavy component to run — justified only at this scale.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Unchanged.

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.why: Unchanged; still absorbs most global traffic.

nodes.label: Load Balancer + Rate Limiter
nodes.why: Rate limiting from step 4 folded into the entry tier; the counters still live in Redis.

nodes.label: Redis Cluster
nodes.why: Clustered so the cache itself is partitioned across nodes as the hot set grows.

nodes.label: API Server 1
nodes.why: Routes each code to its shard by hash and publishes a click event instead of updating a counter row.

nodes.label: API Server N
nodes.why: Same shard-routing logic; the fleet scales independently of storage.

nodes.label: Kafka
nodes.why: Durable, partitioned log that accepts millions of small events per minute and lets analytics replay history.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL Shard 1
nodes.why: Owns id range and rows for its hash bucket; each shard keeps its own replicas as in step 4.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL Shard N
nodes.why: Adding a shard adds write throughput and disk; consistent hashing limits how many keys move when it happens.

nodes.label: Analytics Consumer
nodes.why: Consumes click events in batches and writes per-link counts and dashboards to its own store, off the redirect path.

textAlternative: Five diagrams show a URL shortener growing. Step 1: a client talks to one API server backed by one PostgreSQL database. Step 2: a load balancer distributes requests across several API servers that share the database and claim id ranges for base62 codes. Step 3: a Redis cache sits beside the database so most redirects are answered from memory. Step 4: a CDN caches redirects at the edge, a rate limiter backed by Redis protects the entry point, and PostgreSQL read replicas take cache-miss reads. Step 5: the database is sharded by hash of the code, Redis becomes a cluster, and every redirect publishes a click event to Kafka for an analytics consumer.
